title: Kabir's saloks
hook: near the Granth's end come over two hundred short couplets of Kabir, sharp and funny (ang 1364–1377)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kabir on the death the world fears. Your line was what they fear, I welcome. Did you meet one small fear for a breath instead of running? Today, Kabir at his shortest and sharpest. Day two hundred fifty-seven.

Some of the most-shared words in the world are the shortest. A proverb your grandmother said once, that you still hear at thirty. A line on a sticky note on the fridge. Two sentences someone posts that everybody screenshots. Short things stick, because you can carry them. Near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib there's a whole run of Kabir's short sayings, two lines each, a couple of hundred of them, some tender, some sharp enough to sting, some genuinely funny. Today's word is what they're called: salok.
screen: `GRANDMOTHER'S PROVERB.` → `A NOTE ON THE FRIDGE.` → `SHORT THINGS STICK.`

segments.voice: A salok is a short verse, usually a couplet; the word comes from the Sanskrit shloka. Kabir's saloks fill the pages from Ang 1364 to 1377, and there are more than two hundred of them. A few, marked with the Gurus' names, are replies or comments by Guru Amar Das and Guru Arjan, tucked in among his. Each one usually opens with his own name, Kabir, like a signature on a postcard. Here are three, in paraphrase. The very first: Kabir, my rosary is my tongue, and on it is God's Name. No beads needed; the prayer is in how you speak. Another: Kabir, I'm the worst of all; everyone else is good. Whoever understands it this way is my friend. That's a joke with a point. The quickest way to stop judging people is to start with yourself. And another: a true saint doesn't give up goodness even among a crowd of bad people, just as the sandalwood tree, wrapped in snakes, never stops being cool and fragrant. Notice the pattern. Each salok takes one ordinary picture, a tongue, a mirror, a tree, and flips it. They're built to be memorized, to be quoted at the right moment, to sting a little and then stay with you. That's why this part of the Granth is so loved. Many Sikhs know a handful by heart, the way other people know proverbs. You don't have to read all two hundred. Three, carried well, will do.
screen: `SALOK — A SHORT COUPLET.` · `ANG 1364–1377: OVER TWO HUNDRED.` · `ROSARY, MIRROR, SANDALWOOD.` · `ONE PICTURE, FLIPPED.` · then, large: `SHARP AND SHORT.`

segments.voice: Take the three saloks with you into the quiet. First: my rosary is my tongue. Let the breath go in and out, and notice how you've spoken today. Second: I'm the worst of all; everyone else is good. Let that soften one judgment you're carrying. Third: the sandalwood stays cool, even among snakes. Picture yourself staying kind in one hard place. Rest with whichever one stays. The bell holds the time.
Salok. A short verse, usually a couplet; Kabir's more than two hundred saloks near the Granth's end are sharp, short, and made to be remembered.
Your line: sharp and short. Today, keep one of the three saloks in your pocket, and use it once when the moment comes. Day two hundred fifty-seven.
